parts.title: Watching badgers with my grandfather
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
My grandfather has watched badgers for forty years, and last summer he finally invited me to go with him. I thought it would be boring, but I agreed, because I wanted to impress him.

We left the house at half past eight and walked to a small wood behind the farm. My grandfather told me to wear dark clothes and to be silent. 'Badgers have terrible eyesight,' he whispered, 'but their hearing and sense of smell are excellent.' We sat on the ground for an hour, and nothing happened. My legs hurt, and I was cold.

Then, just as I was about to say that we should go home, a small black-and-white face appeared from a hole under a tree. Another followed, and then three tiny young badgers came out and began to roll around on the grass like puppies. I forgot about the cold completely.

On the way home, my grandfather said that he had watched the same family for years, but that it was always special. I understood what he meant. Now I go with him every Friday, and he has promised to teach me how to take photographs in the dark.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer agree to go?
options: He loves being outside at night
questions.explanation: He thought it would be boring but agreed because he wanted to impress his grandfather.

questions.prompt: What did his grandfather say about badgers?
options: They only come out in winter
They are easy to see in the dark
questions.explanation: Badgers have terrible eyesight, but their hearing and sense of smell are excellent.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel during the first hour?
questions.explanation: His legs hurt, he was cold, and nothing happened.

questions.prompt: What happened just before they went home?
options: Young badgers came out of a hole
A fox ran across the grass
questions.explanation: A face appeared from a hole, and then three young badgers began to play on the grass.

questions.prompt: What does the writer do now?
options: Takes photos for a nature magazine
questions.explanation: He goes with his grandfather every Friday.

parts.title: Beavers return to the valley
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
For about four hundred years, there were no beavers in this part of the country. [1] Last spring, however, two pairs were released into a quiet river valley, and the results have surprised everyone.

Beavers are famous builders. They cut down small trees with their strong teeth and use them to build dams across streams. [2] The pools behind the dams are home to fish, frogs and insects that could not live there before.

Not everyone was pleased at first. Some farmers were afraid that the water would flood their fields. [3] The project manager, Dr Karim Dale, visited each farm to explain the plan, and he promised to move the beavers if there were any problems.

So far, there have been none. In fact, one farmer has said that the new pools are useful for his cows in dry weather. [4] Visitors can now watch the animals from a wooden platform, although they must be quiet. [5] 'Most people are happy just to see the signs of beavers,' says Dr Dale, 'because they are very shy, especially in daytime.'
sentences: These dams slow the water and make new pools.
Seeing a beaver is not easy, though.
Some even asked the council to stop the project.
The first beavers arrived by lorry in large wooden boxes.
They had been hunted until the last one disappeared.
The area has also become popular with tourists.
They will be moved next year to a bigger forest.
Since then, the farmers have refused to speak to Dr Dale.

gaps.explanation: The sentence explains why there were no beavers, and "however" in the next sentence shows the change last spring.
The sentence explains what the dams do, and the next sentence talks about the pools behind them.
The sentence shows how strongly some farmers felt, and the next sentence says that Dr Dale visited each farm.
The sentence says the area attracts tourists, and the next sentence describes the platform where visitors watch.
The sentence says that seeing a beaver is difficult, and the manager then says that people enjoy seeing signs of them.

parts.title: A day at a nature reserve
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage:
On Sunday, my class went to a nature reserve near the coast. We arrived at nine o'clock, and the warden, Mr Cole, [1] us at the gate. He explained the rules and gave each of us a leaflet [2] pictures of the birds that live there. First, we walked along a path through the sand dunes, [3] we saw rabbits and lizards. Mr Cole asked us to talk quietly, [4] we could see more animals. 'If you make a lot of noise, wild animals [5] away,' he said.

After lunch, we sat in a hide, a small wooden hut, and watched the birds through binoculars. I counted [6] than fifty ducks!

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: The story is in the past, so the past form "met" is needed.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: A leaflet "with pictures" is a leaflet that has pictures.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: "Where" refers to the place, the sand dunes.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: "So" shows the purpose: to see more animals.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: The subject "wild animals" is plural and the sentence is in the present.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: "More than fifty" is the usual way to say over fifty.

parts.title: A leaflet for visitors
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Welcome to Lakeside Nature Reserve! The reserve is open every day [1] sunrise to sunset. Please keep to the paths, [2] you may damage the plants. Dogs are welcome, but they must stay [3] a lead. You can see more than a hundred kinds of birds here, [4] ducks, swans and herons. Visitors are not [5] to pick flowers or feed the animals. If you have [6] questions, our staff will be happy to help you.

gaps.explanation: The expression "from sunrise to sunset" gives the opening hours.
"Or" means "if you do not", as a warning.
Dogs must stay on a lead.
The rule says that picking flowers is not allowed.
"Any questions" is the usual polite phrase.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: colm
turns.text: Good morning. How can I help you?

turns.speaker: rhoswen
turns.text: Two tickets for the zoo, please. One for me and one for my daughter. She’s eight.

turns.speaker: colm
turns.text: An adult ticket is twelve pounds, and children under ten pay six. There’s also a family ticket for twenty-four pounds, but that’s for four people, so it isn’t worth it for you.

turns.speaker: rhoswen
turns.text: No, that’s too much for just the two of us. Does she really have to pay? She’s tall for her age.

turns.speaker: colm
turns.text: I’m afraid so. She’s under ten, so it’s the same price as any other child. Would you like a free map?

turns.speaker: rhoswen
turns.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

question.prompt: How much will the woman and her daughter pay in total?
question.explanation: The adult ticket costs twelve and the family ticket twenty-four, but the daughter is under ten and pays the child price, so they pay twelve plus six.

turns.speaker: hester
turns.text: Good morning, visitors, and welcome to Seabay Wildlife Park. A short message about today’s seal trip. Our boat normally leaves at ten o’clock, and many of you have booked that time. Unfortunately, the captain has to collect fuel this morning, so the first trip will leave an hour later than usual. We had thought of moving it to the afternoon, but the tide is wrong after one. There was also an idea of a twelve o’clock trip, but that boat is already full with a school group. So please come to the harbour gate a little before the new time. Seals are very active just then. Thank you for your patience.

question.prompt: What time does the seal trip leave today?
question.explanation: The trip usually leaves at ten, but because of the fuel it will leave one hour later; the afternoon and the full noon boat were rejected.

turns.speaker: morgan
turns.text: Tilly, which animal did you like best today? The elephants were huge.

turns.speaker: tilly
turns.text: They were amazing, and I took a hundred photos of them, but then I got a bit bored. I’d planned to love the penguins most. I’ve wanted to see them for years. But they were asleep all afternoon.

turns.speaker: morgan
turns.text: What about the ones on the hill?

turns.speaker: tilly
turns.text: Oh, those! I nearly bought a toy one in the shop. They kept stealing each other’s food and chasing each other round. I laughed so much that I couldn’t take any photos. That was my favourite bit of the day.

question.prompt: Which animal does Tilly like best?
question.explanation: She was bored with the elephants and the penguins were asleep; the animals on the hill, the monkeys, made her laugh and she nearly bought a toy one.

turns.speaker: delia
turns.text: Quincy, I’m looking for my binoculars. Did you see them anywhere?

turns.speaker: quincy
turns.text: I saw a pair by the lake this morning, on a bench, but I think they belonged to a man with a green hat. Were yours black?

turns.speaker: delia
turns.text: Yes, mine are black with a red strap. I was in the car park earlier, so I’ll look there too.

turns.speaker: quincy
turns.text: Wait. I saw another pair on a table next to a cup of tea. A red strap, I’m sure.

turns.speaker: delia
turns.text: That must be mine! I had a coffee there after the walk.

turns.speaker: quincy
turns.text: Go quickly before somebody takes them.

question.explanation: The pair by the lake belonged to a man in a green hat; the black ones with a red strap were next to a cup of tea, in the place where she had a coffee.

turns.speaker: mairi
turns.text: Jarrah, are we still going to the wetlands on Saturday? The forecast says rain.

turns.speaker: jarrah
turns.text: Yes, I saw that. I haven’t got a waterproof coat, but I could borrow my brother’s, so that doesn’t matter.

turns.speaker: mairi
turns.text: It’s an hour by train, but there’s a direct one.

turns.speaker: jarrah
turns.text: The distance is fine. It’s just that in the rain the birds stay in the reeds and you can’t see anything. We went once and saw nothing but wet grass.

turns.speaker: mairi
turns.text: Hmm, fair. What about Sunday?

turns.speaker: jarrah
turns.text: Sunday is supposed to be dry. Let’s wait for that.

question.prompt: Why is Jarrah not keen to go on Saturday?
options: It is too far to travel
question.explanation: He can borrow a coat and the journey is fine; his problem is that the birds stay hidden in the reeds when it rains.

turns.speaker: lettice
turns.text: Welcome to Monkey Hill. Before we go in, a few rules. Please keep your bags closed. And please do not feed the monkeys, even if they look hungry and come right up to you. Some people think it’s safer to give them something, or the animals might bite you. That’s not true. Our monkeys are very gentle. But human food, like crisps, biscuits or sweets, is terrible for their stomachs, and last summer two of them were ill for a week because of it. We do sell a special bag of fruit at the shop, but it is only for the keepers, not for visitors. Thank you, and enjoy the visit.

question.prompt: Why must visitors not feed the monkeys?
options: Human food can make them ill
question.explanation: The monkeys are gentle, so biting is not the reason, and the special fruit is for the keepers; human food made two monkeys ill.

turns.speaker: gwenllian
turns.text: Silvio, about the seals. The website says Saturday morning at seven.

turns.speaker: silvio
turns.text: That’s what I thought too, but I phoned them, and they said the early boat is only in summer. In winter there’s one at half past two.

turns.speaker: gwenllian
turns.text: Half past two on Saturday?

turns.speaker: silvio
turns.text: Yes, in the afternoon. Sunday is at ten, but you said you’re at your gran’s then.

turns.speaker: gwenllian
turns.text: Right, I’m there all morning. Then Saturday it is. I’ll tell the others.

question.prompt: When will they see the seals?
question.explanation: The website was out of date for the early boat, and Sunday is when she visits her gran, so they go on the Saturday boat at half past two.

parts.title: Understanding the main idea

turns.speaker: aoife
turns.text: Ward, look! I found a small bird in the garden. It can’t fly.

turns.speaker: ward
turns.text: Poor thing. What are you going to do?

turns.speaker: aoife

turns.speaker: ward
turns.text: Bread isn’t good for them, honestly. And it will be frightened if you keep touching it.

turns.speaker: aoife
turns.text: Should I take it to a vet, then? There’s one near the station.

turns.speaker: ward
turns.text: A vet might be right if it was bleeding, but this one looks fine. It’s probably a young bird learning to fly, and its parents are nearby.

turns.speaker: aoife
turns.text: So you think I should do nothing?

turns.speaker: ward
turns.text: Just keep the cat inside and watch from the window. Leave it alone for a few hours.

options: Give the bird bread and water
Take the bird to a vet at once
question.explanation: He says that bread is not good, a vet is only for a bleeding bird, and the young bird’s parents are near, so they should watch and leave it alone.

turns.speaker: adaline
turns.text: Did you watch the whale programme last night, Roderick?

turns.speaker: roderick
turns.text: I did. The pictures were stunning, especially the ones under the water.

turns.speaker: adaline
turns.text: I know! And it was nearly two hours, but I didn’t notice the time.

turns.speaker: roderick
turns.text: Me neither. Honestly, I could have watched three. What I couldn’t stand was the music.

turns.speaker: adaline
turns.text: Really? I thought it was quite nice.

turns.speaker: roderick
turns.text: It was so loud and dramatic that I couldn’t hear the commentator half of the time. I turned the volume down.

turns.speaker: adaline
turns.text: Oh, I hadn’t realised it bothered you.

question.prompt: What did Roderick dislike about the programme?
question.explanation: He loved the pictures and did not mind the length, but the loud, dramatic music stopped him hearing the commentator.

turns.speaker: marielle
turns.text: Excuse me, Mr Penn. Is it true that the council wants to build a new path through the reserve?

turns.speaker: penn
turns.text: Yes, and I’m against it.

turns.speaker: marielle
turns.text: Really? It would make it easier for visitors with pushchairs.

turns.speaker: penn
turns.text: I agree, and the cost isn’t the issue. The council pays. But the birds nest in that corner in spring. People and dogs would frighten them away.

turns.speaker: marielle
turns.text: Couldn’t you close it in the nesting season?

turns.speaker: penn
turns.text: We could try, but who would check? I think the old path is enough.

turns.speaker: marielle
turns.text: Fair. Thanks, I’ll sign your petition.

question.prompt: What does Mr Penn think about the new path?
options: It would cost too much money
It would be too hard for visitors
question.explanation: He agrees the path would help visitors and the council would pay, but the birds nest there and people and dogs would frighten them.

turns.speaker: casey
turns.text: Torin, shall we go to the beach on Saturday?

turns.speaker: torin
turns.text: The forecast is awful. Wind and rain all day.

turns.speaker: casey
turns.text: The zoo, then? It’s cheap on Saturdays.

turns.speaker: torin
turns.text: Most of it is outdoors, and it’s an hour away. I’d hate to stand in the rain looking at wet lions.

turns.speaker: casey
turns.text: Good point. What about the aquarium? It’s twice the price, and it’s farther than the beach.

turns.speaker: torin
turns.text: True, but everything’s inside, so it doesn’t matter what the weather is doing.

turns.speaker: casey
turns.text: OK, you’ve convinced me. We’ll stay dry all day.

question.prompt: Why do Casey and Torin choose the aquarium?
options: It is cheaper than the other places
It is closer to their homes
It is open whatever the weather
question.explanation: The aquarium costs more and is farther away, but everything is inside, so the weather does not matter.

turns.speaker: kenzo
turns.text: Rubina, you look upset. Is it your cat?

turns.speaker: rubina
turns.text: Not really. Mimi’s healthy, the vet checked her last week, and she never goes far from the house. It’s what she brings home. Yesterday she caught a little bird, in the kitchen.

turns.speaker: kenzo
turns.text: Cats do that.

turns.speaker: rubina
turns.text: I know, but I feel terrible. There are so many birds in our street, and I put out seeds for them in winter.

turns.speaker: kenzo
turns.text: Have you tried a bell on her collar?

turns.speaker: rubina
turns.text: Yes, but she learned to move without making a sound.

turns.speaker: kenzo
turns.text: Hmm. Keep her inside in the morning, when birds are busiest?

turns.speaker: rubina
turns.text: Good idea. I’ll try that.

question.explanation: The cat is healthy and stays near home; Rubina feels terrible because the cat caught a bird in the kitchen.

turns.speaker: terence
turns.text: Vanessa, I hear you’re going on safari. Is it for your photography job?

turns.speaker: vanessa
turns.text: People think so, but no. I’ll take the camera, but only for fun. My boss didn’t ask me.

turns.speaker: terence
turns.text: Do you have friends there?

turns.speaker: vanessa
turns.text: My cousin lives in Nairobi, and it will be lovely to see her, but that’s not why I’m going. When I was little, my dad showed me a film of lions walking across the grassland at sunset. I promised myself I’d see them in the wild one day.

turns.speaker: terence
turns.text: Wow. That’s a dream.

turns.speaker: vanessa
turns.text: Exactly. I’ve saved for three years.

question.prompt: Why does Vanessa want to go on safari?
options: To see lions in the wild
question.explanation: The camera is just for fun and the cousin is a bonus; her dream since childhood is to see lions in the wild.

parts.title: Welcome to the wetland reserve
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: bertrand
turns.text: Good morning, and welcome to Marshfield Wetland Reserve. My name is Bertrand, and I’m the head warden. The reserve is open daily from eight in the morning. In summer we close at seven, but at this time of year it gets dark early, so we lock the gates at five. Please be back at the entrance by then. Now, tickets. An adult ticket costs four pounds. Last year it was three, and some people tell me they’ve heard it will go up to five next year, but for now four is correct. Children under twelve come in free. Next, the hides. We have three of them. The biggest is by the lake, and people like it, but for kingfishers go to the small hide near the entrance. It’s only two minutes from the car park, and the birds sit on the branch above the stream. The one at the far end is good for ducks, not for kingfishers. If you’d like to learn more, we have guided walks. They used to be on Sundays, but now they take place every Saturday, starting at ten in the morning and lasting about an hour. There’s no need to book. Many visitors forget their binoculars. If that’s you, don’t worry. You can hire a pair from the shop, next to the café. Some people think the café has them, but it only sells coffee and cakes. Finally, what will you see? Herons and swans, almost every day. Early in the morning, if you’re lucky and quiet, you can see an otter. Most people expect the most exciting animal to be a deer, but those are in the woods, not near the water. The otters swim near the lake just after dawn. Thank you, and enjoy your visit.

gaps.prompt: In winter the reserve closes at ___
gaps.explanation: Summer closing time is seven, but in winter they lock the gates at five.
It was three last year and may be five next year, but now it is four.

gaps.prompt: For kingfishers, choose the hide close to the ___
gaps.explanation: The big hide is by the lake and the far one is for ducks; the kingfisher hide is near the entrance.

gaps.prompt: There are guided walks every ___ morning
gaps.explanation: They used to be on Sundays, but now they take place every Saturday.

gaps.prompt: You can hire binoculars from the ___
gaps.explanation: The café only sells coffee and cakes; the binoculars come from the shop.

gaps.prompt: Early in the morning, visitors may see an ___
gaps.explanation: Deer are in the woods, but otters swim near the lake just after dawn.

parts.title: A wildlife photographer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: anneka
turns.text: Dirk, how did you start taking photographs?

turns.speaker: dirk
turns.text: I didn’t join the photography club at school. I tried, but it met on the same day as football. My father gave me his old camera when I was ten, the kind with a long lens, and I took it into the garden the very next day. A magazine in the library helped me later, but the camera came first.

turns.speaker: anneka
turns.text: What’s the hardest part of your job?

turns.speaker: dirk
turns.text: People think it’s the bags. Yes, my equipment weighs twenty kilos, but you get used to that. And the long flights aren’t pleasant, though I love seeing new places. The real challenge is patience. Animals do what they want, and you wait, sometimes for days, in the cold, without moving.

turns.speaker: anneka
turns.text: Tell us about your eagle photo.

turns.speaker: dirk
turns.text: That’s the one I’m proudest of. I waited nine days on a cliff in Scotland. The picture didn’t win a prize, and I didn’t mind that, and I wasn’t in danger, the cliff was safe enough. But the eagle only stayed in view for ninety seconds, and I had to be ready in that very short time. That’s why I remember it so well.

turns.speaker: anneka
turns.text: Do you ever feel in danger?

turns.speaker: dirk
turns.text: People ask me that all the time. I’ve had a few small injuries, a bite from a monkey once, but nothing serious. Elephants look scary, though I’m more worried about driving on bad roads. Most animals want to stay away from us. If you stay calm and respectful, they usually walk away.

turns.speaker: anneka
turns.text: What do you hope people feel when they see your photos?

turns.speaker: dirk
turns.text: The colours are nice, and I like it when people say wow, but that isn’t my aim. Fear? No, I never want people to be afraid of animals. They aren’t monsters. I hope people think, I want to look after this. My photos are a way to say that the planet is beautiful and that we could lose it.

turns.speaker: anneka
turns.text: What advice would you give to young people?

turns.speaker: dirk
turns.text: You don’t need an expensive camera. Mine was cheap and second-hand for the first five years. Travelling is great, but it’s not the first step. Begin in your own garden or the park near your house. Watch a bird for an hour. You’ll learn how animals behave, and that will make your photos better.

questions.prompt: How did Dirk start taking photographs?
options: His father gave him a camera
He found a magazine in a library
questions.explanation: He tried the club but it clashed with football; his father gave him a camera at ten, and the magazine came later.

questions.prompt: What does he say is the hardest part of his job?
questions.explanation: The bags are heavy and the flights are not nice, but the real challenge is patience while waiting for the animals.

questions.prompt: Why does he remember the eagle photo so well?
options: The bird stayed for a very short time
He was in danger on the cliff
questions.explanation: The picture won nothing and the cliff was safe; he waited nine days for only ninety seconds.

questions.prompt: What does he say about danger?
questions.explanation: He has had a few small injuries only, he worries more about bad roads than elephants, and most animals want to stay away.

questions.prompt: What does he hope people feel when they see his photos?
questions.explanation: He likes the wow but that is not his aim, he does not want fear; he hopes people want to look after the planet.

questions.prompt: What advice does he give to young people?
questions.explanation: He says an expensive camera is not needed and travelling is not the first step; begin in your garden or park.

parts.title: Getting to know you
parts.instructions: Answer each question in your own words. Aim to speak for 20-30 seconds.

questions.prompt: Do you like animals? Which ones do you like best?
Have you ever visited a zoo or a nature reserve?
Tell me about a walk that you have done in the countryside.
Would you like to have a pet? Why or why not?
